Independent coordinates after a linear constraint

Question 5. Independent coordinates after a linear constraint — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · exact calculation and proof extension

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q41; Phd_CS_1404_Q30. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Find the dimension of the real vector space of symmetric n -by- n matrices with trace zero. Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

Construct an explicit basis, prove spanning and independence, and explain rank versus the number of displayed equations. Handle the dimension-one boundary.

1.
10
2.
14
3.
24
4.
15
Read the complete derivation, checks, and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

For n=5, symmetry leaves five diagonal plus ten upper-triangular parameters. Trace removes one diagonal freedom, leaving 10+4=14, option 2. The alternatives 24, 15, and 10 respectively impose trace on all matrices without symmetry, omit trace, or impose a zero diagonal instead of a zero trace. A diagonal matrix with entries (1,-1,0,0,0) witnesses the last distinction.

Derivation and transfer

A symmetric real n -by- n matrix is specified by n diagonal entries and (n2) upper-triangular entries. The lower-triangular entries are copies, not extra degrees of freedom. Therefore its unconstrained dimension is n(n+1)/2. Trace zero gives one independent homogeneous equation, because the trace functional is nonzero: it takes value one on E11. Choose the first n-1 diagonal entries freely and set the last to their negative sum.

An explicit basis consists of Eij+Eji for i<j and Eii-Enn for i<n. Off-diagonal entries show independence of the first family; the first n-1 diagonal entries then show independence of the second. Every symmetric trace-zero matrix is their unique linear combination. This proves

dimW=(n2)+(n-1)=n(n+1)2-1(n≥1).

At n=1, only the zero matrix remains and the basis is empty. At size zero, there is already a zero-dimensional space and no rank-one trace restriction, so the displayed subtraction is not used. Repeating the trace equation or multiplying it by a nonzero scalar does not add constraints. Requiring every diagonal entry to vanish is stronger than trace zero: the diagonal entries 1 and -1 can cancel.

Question 7. Independent coordinates after a linear constraint — symbolic generalization

n2-1

Read the complete derivation, checks, and option analysis

Correct option: 4.

Option 4 is n(n+1)/2-1 throughout the positive-integer domain. The alternatives n2-1, n(n+1)/2, and n(n-1)/2 respectively discard symmetry, discard trace zero, and replace it by zero diagonal. Derivation and transfer

A symmetric real n -by- n matrix is specified by n diagonal entries and (n2) upper-triangular entries. The lower-triangular entries are copies, not extra degrees of freedom. Therefore its unconstrained dimension is n(n+1)/2. Trace zero gives one independent homogeneous equation, because the trace functional is nonzero: it takes value one on E11. Choose the first n-1 diagonal entries freely and set the last to their negative sum.

An explicit basis consists of Eij+Eji for i<j and Eii-Enn for i<n. Off-diagonal entries show independence of the first family; the first n-1 diagonal entries then show independence of the second. Every symmetric trace-zero matrix is their unique linear combination. This proves

dimW=(n2)+(n-1)=n(n+1)2-1(n≥1).

At n=1, only the zero matrix remains and the basis is empty. At size zero, there is already a zero-dimensional space and no rank-one trace restriction, so the displayed subtraction is not used. Repeating the trace equation or multiplying it by a nonzero scalar does not add constraints. Requiring every diagonal entry to vanish is stronger than trace zero: the diagonal entries 1 and -1 can cancel.

A dimension formula with a prescribed sum space

Question 9. A dimension formula with a prescribed sum space — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · exact calculation and proof extension

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q41; Phd_CS_1404_Q30. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Two subspaces each have dimension 2n, and their sum is a 3n -dimensional space. Find their intersection dimension. Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

Prove the sum/intersection dimension identity and construct subspaces attaining the supplied dimensions. Explain the distinction between union, sum, ambient feasibility and a fixed embedding.

1.
0
2.
10
3.
15
4.
5
Read the complete derivation, checks, and option analysis

Correct option: 4.

At n=5, both subspaces have dimension ten and their sum has dimension fifteen. The identity gives dim(U∩V)=10+10-15=5, option 4. A zero intersection would make the sum dimension twenty; intersection dimension ten would make U and V equal with sum ten; fifteen exceeds either subspace dimension. Thus each distractor contradicts a different supplied constraint.

Derivation and transfer

To justify the sum formula, start with a basis of U∩V of size r. Extend it separately to bases of U and V, of sizes p and q. The union of the shared basis and the two added lists spans U+V. It is independent: a zero relation puts the combination of U-only added vectors in both U and V; expressing it in the shared basis and using independence in U forces its added coefficients to vanish. Independence in V then forces the other coefficients to vanish. Hence

dim(U+V)=p+q-r.

With p=q=2n and sum dimension 3n, r=4n-3n=n. Attainability is constructive: in ℝ3n, let U=span(e1,…,e2n) and V=span(en+1,…,e3n). Their intersection has basis en+1,…,e2n.

If the sum dimension is unspecified, equal individual dimensions do not determine overlap. They can coincide, or have smaller intersection when the ambient dimension permits. In an ambient space of dimension d, necessarily max(0,p+q-d)≤r≤min(p,q). An embedding that preserves the actual U and V does not change their intersection; relative position and the feasible ambient dimension are separate issues.

A rectangular map and its actual domain

Question 13. A rectangular map and its actual domain — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · exact calculation and proof extension

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q41; Phd_CS_1404_Q30. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

A matrix has n+3 rows, n+1 columns and rank n-1. Find its nullity. Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

Prove rank–nullity from a kernel-basis extension. Construct a witness matrix and compare the kernel of its transpose, including the smallest feasible parameter.

1.
2
2.
5
3.
6
4.
8
Read the complete derivation, checks, and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

For n=5, A is eight-by-six with rank four. The kernel dimension is 6-4=2, option 1. The alternatives five, six, and eight are respectively the parameter itself, the domain size before subtracting rank, and the codomain size. The explicit witness retains coordinates 1–4 and kills coordinates 5–6; it does not lose all six coordinates.

Derivation and transfer

The matrix acts on column vectors in ℝn+1 and takes values in ℝn+3. Nullity concerns the kernel in the domain, whose dimension is the column count. To prove rank–nullity, take a basis of the kernel and extend it to a basis of the domain. The images of the added vectors span the image because every domain vector has this expansion and kernel terms disappear. Those images are independent: a zero image of an added-vector combination would put it in the kernel, contradicting independence of the extended basis. The number added equals the rank, proving domain dimension equals nullity plus rank.

Consequently

nullityA=(n+1)-(n-1)=2.

The shape is feasible for every n≥1. A concrete witness sends (x1,…,xn+1) to (x1,…,xn-1,0,0,0,0), a vector with n+3 coordinates. Its kernel is spanned by en,en+1. At n=1, this is the zero map from dimension two to dimension four and still has nullity two. The parameter n=0 would require negative rank and is not a valid instance. The transpose has domain dimension n+3 and the same rank, hence nullity four, not two.

Projecting onto a nonunit direction

Question 17. Projecting onto a nonunit direction — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · exact calculation and proof extension

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q41; Phd_CS_1404_Q30. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Project w=(n,1,2) onto the line spanned by u=(1,1,0). Find the squared projection norm. Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

Calculate the coefficient, signed unit component, projected vector and squared length separately. Check the residual and invariance under a nonzero rescaling of the generator.

1.
8
2.
18
3.
30
4.
3
Read the complete derivation, checks, and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

For n=5, w=(5,1,2), c=6/2=3, and p=(3,3,0). Its squared norm is 9+9=18, option 2. The alternatives 30, 3, and 8 count the original squared norm, the coefficient, and the squared projection onto the different line (1,-1,0). Residual (2,-2,2) has squared norm twelve; 30=18+12 checks the orthogonal decomposition.

Derivation and transfer

Let p=cu with u=(1,1,0). Residual orthogonality gives 0=u·(w-cu)=n+1-2c, so c=(n+1)/2 and p=((n+1)/2,(n+1)/2,0). Taking its squared Euclidean norm gives

‖p‖22=2(n+12)2=(n+1)22.

The four related quantities are coefficient c=(n+1)/2, signed component s=(n+1)/2 along the unit direction u/2, vector p=cu, and squared length s2. They are not interchangeable. The residual is ((n-1)/2,(1-n)/2,2), whose dot product with u is zero, so the proposed vector is the actual nearest point on the line.

For any nonzero real scaling v=tu, the coefficient becomes (n+1)/(2t) but multiplying it by tu gives the same p. At scaling zero the formula divides by zero, while projection onto the resulting zero subspace is defined as zero. The expression remains valid for every real n, although the question uses positive integers; at n=-1 the vector is perpendicular to the line and the projection vanishes.

At n=5, r=(2,-2,2), so its squared norm is 4+4+4=12, option 2. The choices 18 and 30 count projected and total squared norms; four counts only the third-coordinate contribution and misses the first two residual coordinates. The check 18+12=30 verifies both the arithmetic and the type of quantity.

Derivation and transfer

Compute the residual itself before invoking any subtraction rule. The projection onto (1,1,0) is ((n+1)/2,(n+1)/2,0). Hence

r=w-p=(n-12,1-n2,2),‖r‖22=(n-1)22+4.

The dot product with the line direction is (n-1)/2+(1-n)/2=0. Therefore the two components are orthogonal and Pythagoras permits the second route

‖r‖22=n2+5-(n+1)22=(n-1)22+4.

The third coordinate contributes an unavoidable four because the target line has third coordinate zero. The first two coordinates contribute another nonnegative term, vanishing only at n=1. Thus the residual is never zero in this family, although its projection can be nonzero. For arbitrary decompositions w=p+r, the exact expansion includes 2p·r; discarding that term is permitted here only after orthogonality is checked. For complex geometry use 2Re⟨p,r⟩ and actual complex orthogonality, not merely a real-looking coordinate picture.

Finding a parameter from an inner-product constraint

Question 25. Finding a parameter from an inner-product constraint — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · exact calculation and proof extension

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q41; Phd_CS_1404_Q30. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

For u=(1,n) and v=(a,2), find the value of a making the vectors perpendicular. Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

Derive the parameter equation from the actual inner product and check every competing value. Compare the answer under a positive weighted inner product.

1.
10
2.
-5
3.
5
4.
-10
Read the complete derivation, checks, and option analysis

Correct option: 4.

For n=5, cancellation requires a+10=0, so a=-10, option 4. Substitution gives products -10 and 10, summing to zero. The choices 10, -5, and 5 give dot products 20, 5, and 15 respectively, so none is perpendicular. The sign is determined by the equation rather than by a length formula.

Derivation and transfer

Under the standard real Euclidean inner product, orthogonality means the sum of coordinate products is zero. For u=(1,n) and v=(a,2),

u·v=a+2n=0⟺a=-2n.

The products in the two coordinates need not vanish separately: they cancel. Both vectors are nonzero because their first and second fixed entries are nonzero, so their angle is indeed a right angle after the dot-product condition is met. A negative dot product would indicate an obtuse angle, not perpendicularity.

The conclusion depends on the metric. Under the positive-definite weighted product ⟨x,y⟩D=4x1y1+x2y2, the equation is 4a+2n=0, giving a=-n/2. For the Euclidean answer a=-2n, this weighted product is -6n, not zero unless n=0. Positivity of the weights gives a valid geometry, but does not preserve every perpendicular pair. In a general linear parameter equation ca+d=0, first check c≠0 before division; if c=0, the constraint is either impossible or satisfied by every a.

Coordinates in a nonstandard basis

Question 29. Coordinates in a nonstandard basis — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · exact calculation and proof extension

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q41; Phd_CS_1404_Q30. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

The basis is b1=(1,1),b2=(1,-1). Find the first basis coordinate of v=(n,2). Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

Reconstruct both basis coordinates, verify uniqueness, and compute the induced coordinate norm from the Gram matrix. Explain the effect of swapping basis order.

1.
32
2.
5
3.
10
4.
72
Read the complete derivation, checks, and option analysis

Correct option: 4.

At n=5, the equations are c1+c2=5 and c1-c2=2. Their solution is (7/2,3/2), so the first coordinate is 7/2, option 4. The distractor 3/2 is the second coordinate; 5 is the first standard coordinate; 10 doubles that coordinate without solving the basis equations. Reconstruction gives (5,2) exactly.

Derivation and transfer

Write v=c1b1+c2b2 in the stated ordered basis. Comparing ordinary coordinates gives c1+c2=n and c1-c2=2. Add the equations to obtain c1=(n+2)/2 and subtract them to obtain c2=(n-2)/2. Reconstruction verifies both entries:

n+22(1,1)+n-22(1,-1)=(n,2).

The coefficient list is unique because a zero combination has both coefficient sum and difference zero, forcing both coefficients to vanish. The basis is orthogonal, but each squared length is two, not one. Thus dot-product extraction must divide by two. A coordinate vector and the represented geometric vector are different objects: their norms satisfy ‖v‖22=2(c12+c22)=n2+4, not simply c12+c22.

Swapping the basis order swaps the two coefficients. Introducing a dependent generator creates multiple representations, whereas changing from one actual basis to another retains uniqueness in each chosen coordinate system. For real n=2 the second coefficient vanishes; this means the vector lies along b1, not that the basis loses independence.

One independent homogeneous equation

Question 33. One independent homogeneous equation — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · exact calculation and proof extension

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q41; Phd_CS_1404_Q30. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

In ℝn+1, find the dimension of vectors whose coordinate sum is zero. Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

Construct a kernel basis and prove unique free-coordinate parameterization. Compare homogeneous and nonzero constant-sum conditions, including the zero-dimensional kernel boundary.

1.
5
2.
6
3.
1
4.
4
Read the complete derivation, checks, and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

For six ambient coordinates, freely choose the first five and use the sixth to cancel their sum. The dimension is five, option 1. The alternatives six, one, and four are the ambient dimension, the rank of the sum functional, and subtraction of an extra nonexistent independent equation. For instance (1,-1,0,0,0,0) belongs and shows that coordinates need not vanish individually.

Derivation and transfer

The homogeneous coordinate-sum equation in ℝn+1 can be solved without elimination machinery: choose x1,…,xn freely and put xn+1=-(x1+…+xn). The parameterization is linear, injective, and reaches every vector with sum zero. Consequently the dimension is n.

The explicit basis is ei-en+1 for 1≤i≤n. Each has sum zero, every solution is their combination with coefficients xi, and inspecting its first n coordinates proves independence. The equation is a nonzero real linear functional of rank one; its kernel dimension therefore agrees with (n+1)-1.

Replacing the right side by a nonzero constant c gives cen+1+W, an affine translate of the homogeneous kernel W. It still has n free parameters but does not contain zero and is not a vector subspace. At n=0, the homogeneous condition on ℝ1 forces its only coordinate to zero; dimension is zero and the basis is empty. Cancellation, rather than individual coordinate vanishing, is the defining restriction.

Option 2 correctly classifies a nonzero constant-sum set as affine. If its right side is six, (6,0,…,0) is feasible but its double has sum twelve and lies outside. Zero is also infeasible. The homogeneous set permits nonzero cancellation vectors and is a subspace. Having the same number of parameters as a subspace does not make an affine translate a vector space under the original operations.

Derivation and transfer

The homogeneous coordinate-sum equation in ℝn+1 can be solved without elimination machinery: choose x1,…,xn freely and put xn+1=-(x1+…+xn). The parameterization is linear, injective, and reaches every vector with sum zero. Consequently the dimension is n.

The explicit basis is ei-en+1 for 1≤i≤n. Each has sum zero, every solution is their combination with coefficients xi, and inspecting its first n coordinates proves independence. The equation is a nonzero real linear functional of rank one; its kernel dimension therefore agrees with (n+1)-1.

Replacing the right side by a nonzero constant c gives cen+1+W, an affine translate of the homogeneous kernel W. It still has n free parameters but does not contain zero and is not a vector subspace. At n=0, the homogeneous condition on ℝ1 forces its only coordinate to zero; dimension is zero and the basis is empty. Cancellation, rather than individual coordinate vanishing, is the defining restriction.

Question 37. Projection onto a nonorthogonal span

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1404_Q31. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Let u=(1,0,1), v=(1,1,0), and w=(1,2,3). What is the orthogonal projection of w onto their span?

1.

(7/3,2/3,5/3).

2.

(1,2,3).

3.

(4,3,4).

4.

(2,1,1).

Read the complete derivation, checks, and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

Solve the Gram equations, not separate projections

Set p=au+bv=(a+b,b,a) with u=(1,0,1) and v=(1,1,0). The dot products are u·u=v·v=2, u·v=1, u·w=4, and v·w=3. Residual orthogonality to both generators gives

(2112)(ab)=(43).

Twice the first equation minus the second gives 3a=5, hence a=5/3. Substitute back to get b=2/3. Therefore p=(7/3,2/3,5/3), option 1, and r=w-p=(-4/3,4/3,4/3). Dotting r with either generator gives zero. Moreover ‖r‖2=16/3, ‖p‖2=26/3, and their sum 14 equals ‖w‖2.

The span satisfies x1=x2+x3. Option 2's w violates this equation. Option 3's (4,3,4) violates it and also fails residual orthogonality. Option 4's (2,1,1) lies in the span, but its residual (-1,1,2) has dot products 1 and 0 with u and v; one zero test is insufficient. The naive sum of separate projections is 2u+(3/2)v=(7/2,3/2,2), which also fails the two residual tests.

The Gram matrix is positive definite: 2a2+2ab+2b2=(a+b)2+a2+b2>0 for nonzero coefficients. This proves uniqueness. For any alternative q in the span, ‖w-q‖2=‖r‖2+‖p-q‖2, proving nearest-point optimality without assuming it from the drawing.

Residual dot u -4/3+4/3=0
Residual dot v -4/3+4/3=0

2/3

2.

2

3.

3

4.

Read the complete derivation, checks, and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

The normal is n=(2,-1,2), with squared length nine. For target X=(1,2,3) the signed plane-equation residual is n·X-4=2-2+6-4=2. Seek the foot as Q=X-tn. Substitution into the plane equation gives 6-9t=4, so t=2/9 and

Q=(59,209,239),X-Q=29(2,-1,2).

The correction has length (2/9)·3=2/3, option 1. Check membership: 2(5/9)-20/9+2(23/9)=36/9=4. Every other plane point differs from Q by a vector perpendicular to n, so Pythagoras proves that no other point is closer.

Option 2's two is the unnormalized equation residual. Option 3's three is the normal length itself. Option 4's 1/3 misses the numerator factor two. Distinguish the coefficient 2/9, distance 2/3, and squared distance 4/9. Scaling the entire equation to 4x-2y+4z=8 doubles both residual and normal length and leaves the distance unchanged. Question 39. Parameter-dependent independence

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q41; Phd_CS_1404_Q32. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Vectors (1,1,0), (1,0,1), and (0,1,a) in ℝ3 are independent exactly when which condition holds?

1.
a≠1
2.
a≠-1
3.
a>0
4.
a≠0
Read the complete derivation, checks, and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

Let the coefficients be r,s,t. A zero combination gives r+s=0, r+t=0, and s+at=0. The first two force s=t=-r; the third is -(1+a)r=0. For a≠-1, this forces all coefficients zero and proves independence, option 2. At a=-1, coefficients (1,-1,-1) give a concrete nontrivial relation.

Option 1 excludes a valid value 1 but includes the invalid value -1. Option 3 unnecessarily requires positivity: zero and -2 are both valid. Option 4 excludes the valid value zero while retaining the invalid value -1. The exceptional parameter is determined by the coefficient equation, not by a sign intuition about coordinates.

The generator matrix has determinant -(a+1), a second calculation consistent with the direct proof. At a=-1, the first two vectors remain independent and the third is their difference, so the rank is exactly two rather than zero or one. Their cross product is (1,-1,-1) and its dot product with the third vector is -(1+a); this is the signed volume whose vanishing detects the same degeneracy. A zero volume need not mean every pair is parallel.

Question 40. An affine minimum norm problem

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1404_Q31; Phd_CS_1404_Q32. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Among real vectors (x,y,z) satisfying x+y+z=6, what is the minimum squared Euclidean norm and where is it attained?

1.

12 at (2,2,2).

2.

36 at (6,0,0).

3.

6 at (1,2,3).

4.

0 at (0,0,0).

Read the complete derivation, checks, and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

The affine constraint is x+y+z=6. Cauchy–Schwarz with normal (1,1,1) gives 36≤3(x2+y2+z2), hence squared norm at least twelve. Equality requires the vector to be a scalar multiple of the normal; its coordinate sum makes that multiple two. The feasible attaining vector is (2,2,2), so option 1 gives the exact minimum and optimizer.

An explicit complete-square certificate is

x2+y2+z2=12+(x-2)2+(y-2)2+(z-2)2

on the constrained plane, because expanding the right side uses x+y+z=6. The extra squares vanish simultaneously only at (2,2,2), proving uniqueness. Option 2's (6,0,0) is feasible but has squared norm 36, not the minimum. Option 3's (1,2,3) has squared norm fourteen rather than six. Option 4's zero vector is not feasible.

For a nonzero real normal a and plane a·x=d, the same argument gives minimum squared norm d2/‖a‖2, attained at da/‖a‖2. If d=0, the minimum is zero at zero. If a is zero, first decide whether the equation is vacuous or inconsistent. A lower bound without a feasible equality case would not complete the optimization.

Question 41. Coordinates are not dot products in a general basis

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q41; Phd_CS_1404_Q31. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

In the basis b1=(1,1), b2=(1,-1), find coordinates of (3,1) and its squared Euclidean norm.

1.

(2,1) and 10.

2.

(4,2) and 20.

3.

(2,1) and 5.

4.

(3,1) and 10.

Read the complete derivation, checks, and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

The coefficient equations are c1+c2=3 and c1-c2=1, giving (c1,c2)=(2,1). Reconstruction gives 2(1,1)+(1,-1)=(3,1). The physical squared norm is 32+12=10, option 1.

The basis Gram matrix is G=(2002), since the two basis vectors are perpendicular but each has norm 2. Thus a coordinate column c has squared norm cTGc=2(22+12)=10. Option 3 correctly finds the coordinates but computes their unweighted squared norm five, assuming a normalized basis. Option 2 uses the raw dot products 4 and 2 as coordinates and would reconstruct (6,2); its reported twenty is not the target's norm. Option 4 retains the standard coordinate tuple instead of converting it to the stated basis.

For a general real basis matrix B, x=Bc implies ‖x‖2=cTBTBc. A nonorthogonal basis produces cross terms in its Gram matrix; an orthogonal nonunit basis produces diagonal weights; only an orthonormal basis produces the identity. Coordinates describe a vector, while the Gram matrix describes its geometry in those coordinates.

Question 42. A complex inner product uses conjugation

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1404_Q31; Phd_CS_1404_Q32. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Using ⟨u,v⟩=∑ui¯vi, let u=(1,i) and v=(i,1). Find ⟨u,v⟩ and ‖u‖2.

1.

0 and 2.

2.

2i and 0.

3.

2i and 2.

4.

0 and 0.

Read the complete derivation, checks, and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

The definition conjugates the first argument. Since 1¯=1 and i¯=-i,

⟨u,v⟩=1·i+(-i)·1=0,‖u‖2=1·1+(-i)i=2.

This is option 1. Option 2 omits conjugation in both calculations, producing 2i and 1+i2=0. Option 3 uses the wrong un-conjugated cross product but the correct norm. Option 4 uses the correct cross product but a bilinear self-product that vanishes for a nonzero vector. Positive definiteness rules out that last purported norm.

Conjugate symmetry gives ⟨v,u⟩=⟨u,v⟩¯=0 here; it does not say the two ordered products always agree. For one-dimensional vectors 1 and i, the products are i and -i. Under the stated convention, the coefficient of projection along a nonzero b is ⟨b,x⟩/⟨b,b⟩. As a diagnostic, projecting x=ib must give coefficient i, whereas using the reversed numerator gives -i and the wrong vector. Every scalar movement and formula must follow the same convention.

Question 43. Equality versus inequality in a projection

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1404_Q31. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

P is orthogonal projection onto a plane through zero in ℝ3. For a nonzero x perpendicular to that plane, what is ‖x-Px‖/‖x‖?

1.

0

2.

1/2

3.

1

4.

It depends on the plane.

Read the complete derivation, checks, and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

Choose an orthonormal basis of the target plane. The assumed nonzero x is perpendicular to each basis vector, so every projection coefficient vanishes and Px=0. Therefore x-Px=x and the requested ratio is one, option 3.

Option 1's zero would describe x lying in the plane. Option 2's one half imposes an unexplained split of its length. Option 4 ignores that the perpendicularity condition fixes the result for every plane. The nonzero assumption ensures the denominator is positive; at x zero the written ratio would be 0/0 and undefined, despite the projection being well-defined.

For arbitrary nonzero x, the orthogonal decomposition gives 0≤‖x-Px‖/‖x‖≤1. The ratio equals zero exactly for vectors in the plane and one exactly for perpendicular vectors, since those cases force one squared component to vanish. Intermediate ratios correspond to a mixture of plane and normal components. For example x=(1,0,1) with the xy-plane gives ratio 1/2, showing why neither a fixed half nor a norm-squared fraction may be substituted for the actual length ratio.

Question 44. Gram geometry and dependence

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1404_Q31; Phd_CS_1404_Q32. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Two real vectors have squared lengths 9 and 16 and dot product 12. Which conclusion follows?

1.

They are independent.

2.

They are perpendicular.

3.

They are dependent and point in the same direction.

4.

Their sum has squared length 25.

Read the complete derivation, checks, and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

The lengths are three and four, and the dot product is twelve. Hence u·v=‖u‖‖v‖>0, equality in Cauchy–Schwarz. A direct residual calculation proves the dependence and its sign:

‖v-43u‖2=16-243·12+169·9=0.

Positive definiteness forces v=(4/3)u, a positive multiple, so they point in the same direction: option 3. Option 1 is contradicted by this nontrivial relation; option 2 would require dot product zero. The squared sum norm is 9+16+24=49, not 25, rejecting option 4. The squared difference norm is 9+16-24=1, an additional check.

The Gram matrix (9121216) has determinant zero and kernel coefficient vector (-4/3,1). If the dot product were -12, dependence would still hold but the scalar would be -4/3 and the directions opposite. A feasible dot product lies in [-12,12]; values beyond these endpoints cannot describe vectors in positive-definite inner-product geometry. Positive individual lengths do not guarantee an independent pair.

Integrated multistep challenges

Question 45. Projection onto a nonorthogonal span

Original integrated challenge · retained after review

Let u=(1,1,0), w=(1,0,1) and v=(0,1,1). What is the Euclidean projection of v onto span(u,w)?

1.
(1,1,1)
2.
(2/3,1/3,1/3)
3.
(0,1/2,1/2)
4.
(1/2,1/2,1/2)
Read the complete derivation, checks, and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

Let p=cu+dw=(c+d,c,d) for the two stated generators. Their squared norms are two, their dot product is one, and their dot products with v are each one. Enforcing both residual orthogonality equations gives 2c+d=1 and c+2d=1. Subtract them to get c=d; then 3c=1. Thus p=(2/3,1/3,1/3), option 2.

The residual is (-2/3,2/3,2/3) and is perpendicular to both generators. Its squared norm is 4/3 while the projection squared norm is 2/3; their sum two equals ‖v‖2. The plane is characterized by first coordinate equal to the sum of the other two. Option 1's (1,1,1) violates this. Option 3's (0,1/2,1/2) and option 4's (1/2,1/2,1/2) also fail membership. The naive sum of separate line projections is (1,1/2,1/2): it lies in the plane, but its residual has dot product -1/2 with each generator, so membership alone does not verify projection.

For any other plane point q, the error separates as ‖v-q‖2=4/3+‖p-q‖2. This proves both optimality and uniqueness. Gram equations keep the nonzero cross inner product that the separate-projection shortcut loses.

Question 46. Minimum norm on an affine intersection

Original integrated challenge · retained after review

Among real (x,y,z) satisfying x+y=1 and y+z=1, what is the minimum squared Euclidean norm?

1.
1/3
2.
2/3
3.
1
4.

Read the complete derivation, checks, and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

Both constraints imply x=z=1-y. Conversely every real y produces a feasible vector, so the entire feasible set is the affine line (1,0,1)+y(-1,1,-1). Its squared norm is

F(y)=2(1-y)2+y2=3(y-23)2+23.

The nonnegative square proves a global lower bound 2/3, attained uniquely at y=2/3, hence x=z=1/3. This is option 2. Option 1's 1/3 omits two coordinate squares at the attaining point. The values one and two can occur elsewhere but are not minimal: y=1 gives one and y=0 gives two. The requested squared norm differs from the actual minimum norm 2/3.

At the minimizing point, the dot product with the line direction is (1/3)(-1)+(2/3)(1)+(1/3)(-1)=0. Thus it is the projection of the origin onto this affine line, providing a geometric proof consistent with completing the square. For a feasible displacement t(-1,1,-1) from it, the squared norm becomes 2/3+3t2, which certifies unique optimality. Solving the constraints first avoids searching over infeasible vectors or treating a nonhomogeneous solution set as a subspace.

Final review: formulas, complete decisions, and boundary tests

Each rule names its geometry and assumptions. Reconstruct the derivation from the full lesson before using this section as a recall sheet. A plotted example illustrates an exact statement; it does not replace its proof.

1. Points and displacements have different roles

The displacement from A to B is B-A; reversing the endpoints negates it. Translation of the origin changes both point-coordinate lists but not their difference. For A=(2,-1,3) and B=(-1,4,5), the displacement is (-3,5,2) and distance 38. Projecting onto an affine line begins with a displacement from its base point, not the target's raw coordinates.

2. A field is part of an independence question

The vectors 1 and i are independent over the reals but dependent over the complex numbers, since i·1-1·i=0. Specify the scalar field before using a dimension count. Zero vectors, repeated vectors, and scalar multiples supply immediate nontrivial relations. Pairwise nonparallel vectors need not form an independent larger list.

3. Span and unique coordinates require separate tests

Write a general linear combination and compare coordinates to test membership. For u=(1,0,1) and v=(0,1,1), the span is z=x+y. Appending u+v changes neither this span nor its dimension, but produces nonunique coefficients. A basis must both span the stated space and be independent.

4. A union is not generally a sum

The two coordinate axes have a union excluding (1,1), while their sum is the plane. A union of subspaces is a subspace precisely when one contains the other. Intersections are always subspaces and contain zero. “Zero intersection” means intersection exactly {0}, not disjoint sets.

5. Sum dimensions subtract the shared basis once

Use dim(U+V)=dimU+dimV-dim(U∩V). Two ten-dimensional subspaces with fifteen-dimensional sum have five-dimensional intersection. Individual dimensions alone do not fix the overlap. In ambient dimension d, require max(0,p+q-d)≤r≤min(p,q) and use a coordinate-basis construction to verify attainability.

6. Constraints remove independent rank

Symmetric real n-by-n matrices have n(n+1)/2 parameters. For n≥1, trace zero removes one, giving n(n+1)/2-1. Five-by-five gives fourteen. Repeated equations add no rank, and trace zero does not force every diagonal entry to vanish. At size zero the trace constraint is already vacuous.

7. Nullity belongs to the domain

For an m-by-k matrix acting on column vectors, dimkerA=k-rankA. An eight-by-six rank-four matrix has nullity two; its transpose has nullity four. Never subtract rank from the row count without changing which map is being discussed. The rank cannot be negative or exceed either dimension.

8. Coordinate norms use the basis Gram matrix

If x=Bc, its squared Euclidean norm is cTBTBc. In the basis (1,1),(1,-1), coordinates (2,1) represent (3,1) and have physical squared norm ten, not five. Orthogonality removes cross terms; unit lengths remove the remaining diagonal weights. Only an orthonormal basis permits the ordinary coordinate-square sum.

9. Squared norms keep their cross term

For real inner-product geometry, ‖x+y‖2=‖x‖2+2⟨x,y⟩+‖y‖2. Lengths three and four with dot product twelve give sum squared length 49. A result of 25 has assumed perpendicularity without evidence. In complex geometry replace the cross term by twice the real part.

10. Cauchy–Schwarz equality means dependence

The bound |⟨x,y⟩|≤‖x‖‖y‖ has equality exactly for dependence over the stated field, including zero cases. With squared lengths nine and sixteen and dot product twelve, v=(4/3)u. A negative endpoint gives the opposite direction. A dot product outside the feasible interval cannot describe such vectors.

11. Triangle equality has a stricter sign condition

Nonzero vectors in inner-product geometry attain ‖x+y‖=‖x‖+‖y‖ only for positive real proportionality. Taking v=-3u gives Cauchy–Schwarz equality but strict triangle inequality. Zero inputs are handled separately. Do not transfer an absolute-value equality condition to a signed sum.

12. Reverse triangle rejects impossible distances

Use |‖x‖-‖y‖|≤‖x-y‖≤‖x‖+‖y‖. Lengths two and three permit distances between one and five in a real space of dimension at least two; in one dimension only the sign cases give one or five. Construct an equality case when an optimization asks for attainability.

13. Zero vectors are orthogonal but have no angle

For nonzero real vectors, cosθ=⟨x,y⟩/(‖x‖‖y‖) and θ∈[0,π]. The zero vector has zero inner product with every vector, but the angle formula divides by zero. The unsigned right angle is π/2, not the negative right-angle value in the corrected Stanford slide.

14. Positive weights define a geometry

The product ∑wixiyi is positive definite on the full real coordinate space when all weights are positive. Zero weights permit a nonzero zero-length vector; negative weights permit negative self-products. With weights (4,1), projecting (1,0) onto (1,1) gives (4/5,4/5) rather than (1/2,1/2). Use the same metric for both coefficient and normalization.

15. Orthogonality is one scalar equation

For (1,n) and (a,2) in Euclidean geometry, the equation is a+2n=0. At n five, a is -10; the two coordinate products cancel. Requiring each product to be zero is stronger and wrong here. Changing the metric to weights (4,1) changes the equation to 4a+2n=0.

16. Complex inner products need a fixed convention

This chapter uses ⟨u,v⟩=∑ui¯vi, linear in v. For (1,i) and (i,1) the product is zero, and the first vector has squared norm two. A bilinear self-product gives zero for that nonzero vector and cannot define its norm. Oxford's opposite convention is translated explicitly.

17. Complex Pythagoras has a one-way converse

Orthogonality implies squared-norm additivity. The converse of a single such equality only gives zero real part of the inner product. The one-dimensional complex vectors 1 and i satisfy |1+i|2=1+1 but have inner product i. Do not infer complex orthogonality from a real-valued expansion alone.

18. Projection coefficient, component, vector, and length differ

For nonzero real b, coefficient is c=(b·x)/‖b‖2, signed unit component is (b·x)/‖b‖, and projected vector is cb. Projecting (5,1,2) onto (1,1,0) gives coefficient three, component 32, vector (3,3,0), and squared length eighteen. State which quantity is requested before computing.

19. Rescaling a nonzero generator preserves its span

Replacing b by tb with t≠0 changes the coefficient to c/t and leaves the projected vector unchanged. At t zero the quotient is undefined, but projection onto the zero subspace is zero. The mathematical object can remain defined after one representation formula fails.

20. A projection answer needs two certificates

Check that p belongs to the target span and that x-p is perpendicular to every generator. In Question 37, (2,1,1) passes membership but fails one residual test. The correct (7/3,2/3,5/3) passes both. These certificates prove unique nearest-point optimality through Pythagorean error decomposition.

21. Nonorthogonal directions require coupled coefficients

Solve Gc=BTx for real independent generators, with G=BTB. For u=(1,0,1), v=(1,1,0) and x=(1,2,3), G=(2112) and c is (5/3,2/3). Summing separate line projections ignores the off-diagonal interaction. With dependent generators the vector can remain unique while its coefficients are nonunique.

22. Orthogonal does not mean orthonormal

An orthogonal nonzero basis needs each denominator ‖uk‖2 in its projection sum. With u=(2,0), the unnormalized source sum produces diag(4,0) rather than a projection. The authentic Q31 wording is therefore marked ambiguous; option three is explained only under an added normalization interpretation. Preserve the source condition rather than silently strengthening it.

23. Idempotence alone does not imply contraction

The oblique map Q=(1200) satisfies Q2=Q but increases the length of (0,1) to two. True orthogonal projection satisfies ‖Px‖≤‖x‖, with equality precisely for x in its image. For the full-space projection every vector has equality.

24. Residual energy and captured energy form a partition

For a true orthogonal projection, ‖x‖2=‖Px‖2+‖x-Px‖2. Question 22 gives 69=81/2+57/2. A squared length cannot be replaced by a coefficient or a length without a square root. For perpendicular nonzero inputs the residual-length ratio is one; for image vectors it is zero.

25. Bessel and Parseval distinguish a list from a complete basis

For an orthonormal list, ∑|⟨qj,x⟩|2≤‖x‖2; the gap is residual squared norm. Two xy-plane directions applied to (2,1,3) capture energy five of fourteen. Equality holds for x in their span; a basis of the entire space gives equality for every x. In complex cases use squared magnitudes.

26. Gram–Schmidt skips a zero residual

Subtract every retained direction's component before normalizing. Inputs (1,1),(2,2),(0,0),(1,-1) produce two unit directions, with the middle two skipped. A zero residual does not force termination of the whole algorithm. A tiny nonzero residual is mathematically independent; numerical decisions need an explicit error scale and tolerance.

27. An affine foot requires translation

For L=P+spanb, project X-P and add P back. For X=(4,0) and P=(1,2),b=(2,1), the foot is (13/5,14/5). Directly projecting X finds a point on a different line through zero. Membership and residual perpendicularity must be checked after translating back.

28. Plane distance uses the normal length once

For a·X=d, distance is |a·X-d|/‖a‖, while the foot correction coefficient divides by ‖a‖2. Question 38 has residual two, normal length three, distance 2/3, and coefficient 2/9. Scaling the entire equation preserves the plane and distance. A zero normal means either the whole space or an inconsistent empty set.

29. Optimization needs feasibility and an attaining case

On x+y+z=6, the unique squared-norm minimum is twelve at (2,2,2). On x+y=1,y+z=1, it is 2/3 at (1/3,2/3,1/3). A complete square proves global optimality, and substitution proves feasibility. A feasible larger value or an unachieved lower bound is not the answer.

30. Norm lower bounds do not imply positive definiteness

A=-I satisfies ‖Ax‖≥‖x‖ in every norm but has a negative quadratic form. For a square map the lower bound does imply invertibility and an induced inverse norm bound. The Frobenius norm is different: In has operator norm one and Frobenius norm n. A magnitude statement is not a positivity statement about eigenvalues or quadratic forms.

31. Parameter endpoints need a null-direction witness

The real symmetric three-by-three matrix with diagonal one and off-diagonal a is positive definite precisely on (-1/2,1). At the lower endpoint its all-equal direction is null; at the upper endpoint its sum-zero plane is null. Outside, one direction has negative quadratic form. For a Gram matrix, determinant zero signals dependence, not merely small vector lengths.

32. Products, polynomial geometry, and parity retain their domains

In oriented real three-space, ‖u×v‖ is parallelogram area, triangle area is half, and |u·(v×w)| is parallelepiped volume. Use side differences from one vertex and retain cross-product parentheses. In polynomial integral geometry, odd functions integrate to zero over symmetric intervals: t3 projects to zero on span(1,t2), and t2-1/3 has squared norm 8/45. Negative cosine frequencies can represent the same function. None of these facts authorizes arbitrary-dimensional cross products or infinite Fourier convergence claims.

Final verification sequence

State the field, ambient space and inner product; check feasibility and every denominator; derive the required vector or scalar; reconstruct coordinates or substitute constraints; check residual orthogonality with the actual metric; compare a second route or boundary. The recorded sources and finite tests support the stated scope. They do not establish a worldwide optimal course selection or a guarantee for every unseen examination question.

13. References and coverage limits

Official course texts used

  1. Stanford University — Stephen Boyd. EE263, Introduction to Linear Dynamical Systems, Autumn 2007–08. Course lecture archive. Linear Algebra Review, all 31 slides reviewed; Orthonormal Sets of Vectors and QR Factorization, all 23 slides reviewed. Full QR factorization theory is deferred.
  2. University of Oxford — M1 Linear Algebra I, Michaelmas 2022. Official 2022–23 course page, instructor Andrew Wathen. Lecture notes, printed pp. 25–43 and 69–77 reviewed. The title page does not individually identify the note author. Row/column conventions and the complex inner-product convention were explicitly reconciled.
  3. University of California, Berkeley — Alexander Paulin. Math 54, Spring 2018. Official course archive. Vectors in Rn; Inner Products, Length and Orthogonality; Orthogonal Projections; Inner Product Spaces. All four handwritten pages of each note were visually reviewed. Tutorial 30 independently corrects the parity error in the final polynomial example.
  4. Massachusetts Institute of Technology — Denis Auroux. 18.02SC Multivariable Calculus, Fall 2010. Official course. Dot Product, instructional pp. 1–2; Components and Projection, instructional p. 1; Cross Product, instructional pp. 1–2. These written notes were read; videos were not required.

The selected texts were compared with candidates from CMU, Cambridge, Harvard, and an ETH-hosted teaching page. Some candidates received only index or sample review; they do not count toward the four genuinely reviewed sources. The separate source audit states exact review levels and access limitations. No assertion is made that every course worldwide was found or that this selection is globally optimal.

What this chapter does and does not establish

The lesson covers the finite-dimensional vector-geometry reasoning patterns listed in its scope, including identified zero, dependence, nonorthogonal, weighted, and complex exceptions. It provides complete proofs of its core projection and inequality claims and worked examples mapped to its topic audit. The new construction sections prove the basis-extension, dimension and Gram-system claims used by this bank. Full matrix factorization, infinite Fourier convergence and advanced numerical rank estimation remain later-chapter topics.

The 34 retained derivation tutorials and 46 separately labeled examination questions are an instructional selection, not every exercise published in the surveyed courses. They include course-derived types in new wording and original diagnostic extensions with full solutions. Original Iranian MSc and PhD questions are now included under the student instruction of 3 October 2026. The four authentic items were checked against the recorded original PDF images; original analogues are not represented as empirical performance calibration. The goal is to eliminate every identified in-scope error and omission; finite checks and source comparisons cannot prove literal perfection or guarantee future performance on every unseen question. This newly revised edition remains a review draft; approval of the earlier edition does not label the new edition student-approved.
